title: Comfy × Valheim — Community Workbench
headline: Seven tools. What each one actually does today, what it costs you to run it, and exactly how to take one over.
honesty_statement: Every status below is what the thing actually does today.
not_a_verdict: This catalog is an invitation to run and own tools. It is not a judgment on anyone's past effort and it is not a verdict on anyone's burnout — volunteers already carried this community, and the work they did is why any of this exists. Nothing here is owed by anyone. A tool sitting unclaimed is a description of this catalog, never a mark against the people who came before.

feedback.rhythm: Replies land in batches, about twice a week — this is a solo-operator project.

ladder.name: Curious
ladder.what_you_did: Read the one-pager for a tool and decided whether it is worth your evening.
ladder.what_you_get: A straight answer about what runs, what does not, and what it would cost you. Reading owes nobody anything.
ladder.recorded_in: Nowhere. There is no sign-up and no list.

ladder.name: Ran it
ladder.what_you_did: Ran the tool locally and posted what happened in its thread — including the part where it broke.
ladder.what_you_get: Named in the thread. A report that it failed is worth exactly as much as a report that it worked.

ladder.name: Fixed one thing
ladder.what_you_did: Completed one of the first tasks listed on a tool card.
ladder.what_you_get: Credited in OWNERS.md, and the tool's ownership state moves to trying.
ladder.recorded_in: OWNERS.md, plus the tool's ownership record.

ladder.name: Steward
ladder.what_you_did: Landed two changes on a tool, or revived a recoverable piece back into something that runs.
ladder.what_you_get: Code access to that piece and you triage its thread. The tool's ownership state moves to claimed.
ladder.recorded_in: OWNERS.md, plus the tool's ownership record.

ladder.name: Owner
ladder.what_you_did: Sustained the stewardship over time, and Derek agrees you are the person holding it.
ladder.what_you_get: You set the tool's direction and you can say no. The ownership state moves to owned.
ladder.recorded_in: OWNERS.md, plus the tool's ownership record.

tools.name: Quest Picker + Absorption Engine
tools.one_liner: Turns a guild's real quest tracker into a single offline page where a player checks the quests they care about — and the game mod reads the result.
tools.status_detail: Runs today against real guild tracker exports: the harvest, the validator, and the picker all work end to end, and the mod reads the quest-view.json the picker saves. The download below is a cold-start kit with a synthetic sample guild — verified to run from a fresh folder with nothing but Python and openpyxl.
tools.what_it_does: Python (standard library, plus openpyxl for .xlsx sources) harvests real guild quest trackers into one JSON catalog per guild. render_quest_picker.py folds a catalog into a single self-contained file:// HTML page with no server and no network calls. A player opens that page, checks the quests they want, and saves a personal quest-view.json that the game mod reads at runtime.
tools.who_its_for: Guild stewards and GMs who already keep a quest tracker and want it to reach players in-game instead of dying in a spreadsheet tab.
requires: A browser — the picker is a local file:// page, not a service

source.note: The same code lives in this repo at recipes/quest-catalogs/ and is byte-identical to the public copy.

first_tasks.done_when: validate.py accepts the file and a GM can author a quest through the gm-template seam without editing harvest.py. sources.json already points at this path (entry rangers-example, currently disabled) but the file has never been written.

first_tasks.done_when: A new catalog JSON renders in the picker and every anomaly the harvest reported has an explanation — zero left unexplained.

tools.privacy_note: Harvested catalogs from a live guild tracker contain member names. The published sample uses synthetic data only — do not commit a real harvested catalog.

tools.name: ComfyStewardView
tools.one_liner: Reads a Valheim world file and answers the questions that stop being walkable once a server gets big: where is everyone building, and who owns this.
tools.status_detail: The public repo builds a fat JAR that parses a real world .db, serves a localhost API, and draws a browser heatmap. It has been used to steward high-player worlds. What is missing is a quickstart for the roughly twenty GM probe utilities — they work, but today you have to read the source to know what each one does.
tools.what_it_does: A Java fat-JAR extracts and parses a Valheim world file (.db), exposes a REST API on localhost:7080 (/api/v1/heatmap, /api/v1/points), and serves a browser heatmap viewer. Around twenty GM probe utilities sit alongside it for build-density clustering and ownership investigation.
tools.who_its_for: Server stewards and GMs on worlds big enough that walking around stopped being a way to find out what is happening.
requires: A copy of a Valheim world .db — a copy, never the live save

source.note: A standalone public repository, separate from baseline. Clone it and build; nothing here is gated.

first_tasks.title: Run it against a copy of any world .db and post one heatmap screenshot
first_tasks.done_when: A heatmap image from your own world is in the thread, with the build command you actually used and anything that tripped you up.

first_tasks.title: Write the missing quickstart for the probe utilities
first_tasks.done_when: Each GM probe utility has one line saying what it answers and one copy-pasteable invocation, and a steward who has never opened the source can pick the right probe from that page alone.

tools.privacy_note: Run it on world copies, not the live save. Output can contain player names — share aggregates and screenshots, not raw dumps.
tools.license: Proprietary — all rights reserved per the repo's own LICENSE.md, which requires written permission and a paid license for reuse. Catalogued here for running it and giving feedback; the license posture is under review, and until it changes, contributions mean docs and feedback, not code redistribution.

tools.name: Live Community Telemetry
tools.one_liner: An aggregates-only telemetry API with privacy tests that fail if a player ID, name, or position ever shows up — plus the whole stack, runnable on your machine.
tools.status_detail: The aggregates API is live on P7 and the public /community page reads it. What is local-only is everything you would need to run or change it yourself: the docker stack that reproduces the whole thing and the loopback operator dashboard both run on your machine, and neither is published as a download.
tools.what_it_does: An aggregates-only v0 telemetry API (GET /api/v0/telemetry/server, /tick, /sessions, /delivery, /regions, /events, /valheim, /cutover) whose test suite asserts that no player ID, name, or position ever appears in a response. A self-contained /community page polls it. A local dev stack brings up the real thing end to end (docker compose: postgres 5435, gateway 4000, eventlog 4002, progression 4003, operatorapi 4004), and a loopback-only operator viewer renders it for a single operator.
tools.who_its_for: Anyone who wants to run the telemetry surface themselves — and anyone who would rather check the privacy claim than take it on faith.
tools.time_to_first_result: about 5 minutes against the live API; about 30 for the local stack once claimed
requires: A browser (or Python 3) for the live aggregates API — that is all CT-1 needs
Docker and docker compose, for the local stack (source access opens at ladder stage 3)
The .NET 9 SDK, only if you want to rebuild the gateway rather than run the composed image

source.note: The code is in this repo — Lumberjacks/infra/docker/docker-compose.yml for the stack, Lumberjacks/tools/omen-dashboard/ for the operator viewer. Access opens at ladder stage 3.

first_tasks.title: Build one chart, tile, or widget from the public v0 API and post it
first_tasks.done_when: Any stack you like — a static page, a spreadsheet, a terminal script — renders live data from a v0 endpoint, and the thread has a screenshot plus how you made it. Needs no repo access; the starter kit includes a Python poller.

first_tasks.title: Bring the local stack up, then add one new aggregate tile the privacy tests still pass on
first_tasks.done_when: The compose stack runs on your machine and a new aggregate is exposed by the v0 API and rendered, with the existing privacy tests passing unmodified. This is the claim path — source access opens at ladder stage 3.

tools.privacy_note: The v0 API is aggregates-only by tested design — no player ID, no name, no position, ever. Keep that bar: a change that makes the privacy tests fail is a change that does not land.
tools.license: BUSL-1.1 with the community-steward safe harbor, converting to AGPL-3.0-only; see LICENSING.md.

tools.name: Steam Self-Service Join
tools.one_liner: An invite link, a Steam sign-in, and a mod-pack zip with your credentials already in it — no config file to hand-edit.
tools.status_detail: The join flow works end to end on comfy-p7.duckdns.org today: invite, Steam sign-in, personalized zip, self-service update and reissue. The operator runbook's own caveats stand and are not softened here — the endpoint is currently plain HTTP on a non-default, world-open port with TLS built and staged but not switched on, rate limiting is not in place yet (the runbook lists it as pre-widening work), it is open to the alpha cohort only, and volunteer platform readiness is recorded as NOT READY. Until TLS is armed, the enrollment credential crosses a plaintext public link.
tools.what_it_does: An invite link opens a page that hands off to Steam OpenID sign-in. A one-use bootstrap token is exchanged for a personalized mod-pack zip with the player's credentials already baked in. Self-service update and reissue run through the same path. The per-player token is stored only as a hash.
tools.who_its_for: The next wave of playtesters — people who want to join and play without being told to edit a config file first.
requires: An invite link from the operator — the endpoint is alpha-cohort only

source.note: Lumberjacks/src/Game.Gateway/Valheim/ in this repo — SteamEnrollmentEndpoints, SteamEnrollmentService, EnrollmentPages, ModpackReleaseCatalog — with real test suites, plus the operator runbook at infra/gcp/p7/VOLUNTEER-ENDPOINT.md. Access opens at ladder stage 3.

tools.name: MCP Mod Channel
tools.one_liner: A localhost MCP server that talks to the running game mod: apply a config profile, run a bounded lab test, read back what happened.
tools.status_detail: It runs, and it really does drive the live mod. It is reachable only from 127.0.0.1 with a dev key, and that is deliberate rather than unfinished: it is a development channel, never a console or shell bridge, and every mutation it can perform is whitelisted and bounded. There is no download and no remote mode.
tools.what_it_does: A local Python MCP server on 127.0.0.1:8720 (header X-Comfy-Key, dev value comfy-dev-local) speaks bidirectionally with the running mod: apply config profiles, run bounded lab motion tests through an atomic mailbox, tail mod telemetry and logs, assemble session bundles, and get local-Ollama explanations of what it just saw.
tools.who_its_for: Mod developers, and anyone curious about wiring an AI tool to a live game process without handing it a shell.
requires: Optional: a local Ollama, only for the explanation tools

source.note: network/mcp/ in this repo — the comfy_gateway kernel plus the valheim toolsurface, contracts/commands.json, and 6 tests. An older snapshot exists in the public comfy repo. Access opens at ladder stage 3.

first_tasks.title: Run the gateway and list its tools from any MCP client, then post the tool list
first_tasks.done_when: The tool list from your own client is in the thread, along with which client you used and anything in the setup that was not obvious.

tools.privacy_note: Bound to 127.0.0.1 on purpose. Do not expose it — it drives a live game process, and its whole safety story is that only you can reach it.

tools.name: Camera Flythrough → Gallery Pipeline
tools.one_liner: Fly a camera along waypoints derived from a world save, then cut the capture into a gallery of what people actually built.
tools.status_detail: Not running. It was pruned from baseline on 2026-07-21 and nothing here executes today. Two of the four segments are real: segment 1 was built and produced real output, and segment 3 has a 746-line working camera proof-of-concept plugin. Segments 2 and 4 are written briefs, not code. Every piece is still in the public comfy repo, so this is a revival rather than a rewrite.
tools.what_it_does: A four-segment pipeline: read a world save, emit camera waypoints via ComfyStewardView, fly those waypoints in-game with a BepInEx camera plugin, then cut the capture into a gallery with ffmpeg.
tools.who_its_for: Anyone who wants to show a server's builds to people who will never log into it.
tools.time_to_first_result: Unknown — nothing runs yet. CG-1 produces the first honest estimate.
requires: Java, for the ComfyStewardView side of segment 1
A BepInEx Valheim install, for segment 3

source.note: Pruned from baseline, but fully preserved in the public comfy repo — nothing was lost.

first_tasks.title: Revive segment 1 against ComfyStewardView and produce a waypoints.sample.json
first_tasks.done_when: segment-1-emit-waypoints.py runs against a current ComfyStewardView build and writes a committed waypoints.sample.json that segment 3 can consume. This is the claiming task for this tool.

recovery.notes: Segment 1 was built and produced real output. Segment 3 has a 746-line working camera proof-of-concept plugin. Segments 2 and 4 are written briefs, not code. The baseline pre-prune ref is cc322ee.

tools.privacy_note: A flythrough shows other people's builds. Ask before publishing a gallery of a world you do not own.
tools.license: MIT — everything recoverable here lives in the public comfy archive, which is MIT-licensed. A revival landing in this repo would land under BUSL-1.1; see LICENSING.md.

tools.name: Quest Submission → Review Bridge
tools.one_liner: The back half of quest capture: package what a player did in-game, land it in a review inbox, and turn it into a record a GM can read.
tools.status_detail: Not running. The front half is alive in the mod today with tests — QuestViewLoader.cs reads a player's quest-view and QuestTriggerEvaluator.cs evaluates triggers in-game. The back half, which packages a submission and turns it into a reviewable record, is not wired to anything; its code sits in the public comfy repo waiting to be pointed at the live mod's telemetry.
tools.what_it_does: Packages an in-game quest submission, lands it in a review inbox, and renders human-readable quest records a GM can act on without chasing screenshots.
tools.who_its_for: GMs who want players to submit completions without a screenshot and a Discord message.
tools.time_to_first_result: Unknown until QB-1 lands. The front half already runs, so the first honest measurement comes from the port.
requires: The mod running locally with quest telemetry enabled
.NET (net48), only if you take the C# submission service rather than the Python consumer

source.note: The back half is preserved in the public comfy repo. The front half is live in this repo's mod at network/mod/ComfyNetworkSense/Core/Services/.

first_tasks.title: Port bridge_consumer.py to read the live mod's quest telemetry and emit one review record
first_tasks.done_when: A real in-game quest completion travels from the running mod through the consumer and comes out as one human-readable review record. This is the claiming task for this tool.

recovery.notes: Front half is alive and tested in the live mod — network/mod/ComfyNetworkSense/Core/Services/QuestViewLoader.cs and QuestTriggerEvaluator.cs. Only the back half needs reviving, and it has fixtures to test against.

tools.privacy_note: A submission record carries a player's name and what they did. Keep the review inbox off any public surface.
tools.license: Split: the live front half (in this repo's mod) is BUSL-1.1 per LICENSING.md; the recoverable back half lives in the public comfy archive under MIT.
